thesis: The market prices a 10% chance the Fed leaves rates unchanged on Dec 9. The claim is that this is too low by a few points, for one mechanism: the thing breaking is itself disinflationary. The selloff is an AI-capex unwind — slowing datacenter buildouts and withdrawn funding for AI projects — and that is a negative investment shock to exactly the industrial, power and labour demand that has kept core inflation sticky. A capex bust does the Fed's work without a hike. Layered on that, financial conditions tightened violently and the move is young: the S&P and Dow entered correction only on Friday, the Nasdaq gave up its entire 2026 gain, and roughly $4 trillion of market value went in five sessions. The pricing itself shows how fast this re-rates — the pause went from essentially nothing pre-Friday to 8-10c in a single session while the 50bp tail was cut from 4.3% to 2-3%. The market is already moving in the direction of this trade, it simply has 12 more sessions of tape to do it in, and a dollar at a 19-month high is importing disinflation that makes waiting one meeting cheap.
key_risk: The base case is firmly a hike and this contract loses in it. October CPI ran +0.35% m/m, the October minutes had almost all officials seeing further increases as appropriate, and the September hike was 12-0 with no dissent at all. Payrolls were +165,000 with unemployment at 4.1% and falling, so there is no labour-market cover for a pause. Pausing would also be read as subordinating the inflation mandate to equity prices, the one thing this Fed has been most insistent it will not do, with the 10-year at 5.04% telling them credibility is the binding constraint. Separately, event-contract specific: fees matter enormously at a 10c entry — Robinhood's panel showed $0.00 but the disclosure says additional fees apply, and a 1-2c round-trip fee moves break-even from 10% to 11-12%, so verify the fill cost before sizing. Finally, 10c is not a claim of Fed autopilot; the price already embeds part of this scenario, so the edge asserted here is 5 points, not a repricing to a coin flip.
counter_argument: The strongest case against: a Fed that has hiked into re-accelerating inflation, unanimously, and told the world in its own minutes that more is coming does not stop because the Nasdaq gave back a year of gains, particularly when unemployment is falling. Equity corrections did not stop hiking cycles in 1994 or 2022 when inflation was the problem. Answered rather than waved away: this trade does not need the Fed to pause. It needs the probability of a pause to be re-rated once, by a tape that already moved it from nothing to 10c in one session, and the exit is 25c rather than resolution for exactly that reason. The honest residual is that if equities simply stabilise over the next fortnight, the contract decays to 4c and the trade is a loss.

The reason to cancel rather than wait is that the macro premise has inverted since publication: a homebuilder long is a leveraged bet on rate relief, and the December meeting is now priced 89% for another 25bp hike against a 3.75-4.00% range, with the 10-year at 5.04% and October CPI running +0.35% m/m. Mortgage rates are not falling on that path. The chart agrees — LEN is 15.9% off its 120-day high with SMA20 at 85.78 above price and an ATR of 4.77% a day. There is also a portfolio reason, which is the stronger one: the Fed-pause event contract captured today is a bet on exactly the rate-relief repricing LEN needs, at 10c with a defined payoff and no equity beta. Holding both is paying twice for one view through the worse of the two instruments.
key_risk: The risk of cancelling is that LEN is already priced for a hiking Fed, so the stock rips if the Fed pauses on Dec 9 and the order is not there to catch it. That is accepted, because the Fed-pause contract already carries that upside more cleanly and with a defined maximum loss. Two honest weaknesses in this call: the evidence is two confirmation kinds rather than three or more, both of them about the vehicle and the macro premise rather than about Lennar's business, which I did not research today; and LEN was recommended twice in the last ten days, which prior_context flags as an anchoring warning rather than a conviction signal — cancelling is how that gets stopped rather than re-litigated a third time. A 4.77% daily ATR also means a bid left working would likely fill on one bad session rather than at a considered level.
counter_argument: The strongest case against cancelling: homebuilders de-rate ahead of the rate cycle and re-rate before cuts arrive, so waiting for the Fed to actually pause means buying 15% higher, and LEN at 0.8x its 120-day range is where that asymmetry lives. Answered on instrument choice rather than on view — the view is not being rejected, the vehicle is. A 10c contract that pays $1 if the Fed pauses expresses the same thesis with a defined maximum loss, whereas LEN expresses it with a 4.77% daily ATR, a downtrend, and no stated catalyst inside the horizon.

evidence.detail: LEN closed 80.74, 15.92% below the 120-day high of 96.03, with SMA20 at 85.78 above price and SMA50 at 81.73 just above. ATR14 3.8507 = 4.77% of price. The published 79.50 entry was missed by 0.185 on 2026-11-19 (low 79.685) and never filled.

The de-rate-early case for owning homebuilders before cuts is answered by instrument choice: the same rate-relief thesis is held today as the Dec 9 Fed-pause contract at 10c with a defined maximum loss, rather than through an equity with a 4.77% daily ATR in a downtrend and no dated catalyst.

thesis: The market prices a 10% chance the Fed leaves rates unchanged on Dec 9. The claim is that this is too low by a few points, on two things the price looks to be underweighting. First, the thing breaking is itself disinflationary: the selloff is an AI-capex unwind — slowing datacenter buildouts and withdrawn funding for AI projects — a negative investment shock to exactly the industrial, power and labour demand that kept core inflation sticky. Second, and this is verifiable rather than narrative, the disinflation is already arriving through energy: US regular gasoline averaged $4.309 in October and $3.984 across the first three weeks of November, -7.55% and still falling, worth roughly -0.3pp on the November CPI index at its basket weight. Layered on that, financial conditions tightened violently and the move is young — the S&P and Dow entered correction only on Friday, the Nasdaq is 20.2% off its high, and roughly $4 trillion of market value went in five sessions. The pricing itself shows how fast this re-rates: the pause went from essentially nothing pre-Friday to 8-10c in one session while the 50bp tail was cut from 4.3% to 2-3%. The market is already moving this way and has 12 more sessions to do it in.
key_risk: The base case is firmly a hike and this contract loses in it. October CPI ran +0.35% m/m, the October minutes had almost all officials seeing further increases as appropriate, the September hike was 12-0 with no dissent, and payrolls were +165,000 with unemployment at 4.1% and falling, so there is no labour-market cover for a pause. The sharpest specific risk is one of sequencing, and it cuts against this trade: the Fed votes on Dec 9 having seen NO official data containing the November energy drop — November CPI lands 12-10, the day after, and November PCE on 12-23. The 11-25 print covers October and may even read firm. So the cleanest argument for waiting is one the committee cannot yet point to in a published statistic, and pausing would read as subordinating the inflation mandate to equity prices with the 10-year at 5.04%. Event-contract specifics matter enormously at a 10c entry: Robinhood's panel showed $0.00 but the disclosure says additional fees apply and the product launched at 2c per contract, so a 1-2c round trip moves break-even from 10% to 11-12% — verify the fill cost before sizing. Finally, 10c is not a claim of Fed autopilot; the price already embeds part of this scenario, so the edge asserted is about 5 points, not a repricing to a coin flip.
counter_argument: The strongest case against: a Fed that has hiked into re-accelerating inflation, unanimously, and told the world in its own minutes that more is coming does not stop because the Nasdaq gave back a year of gains, particularly when unemployment is falling. Equity corrections did not stop hiking cycles in 1994 or 2022 when inflation was the problem. Answered rather than waved away: this trade does not need the Fed to pause. It needs the probability of a pause to be re-rated once, by a tape that already moved it from nothing to 10c in one session, and the exit is 25c rather than resolution for exactly that reason. The honest residual is that if equities simply stabilise over the next fortnight, the contract decays to 4c and the trade is a loss.
